title: Google value plunges by $500bn as AI search hits ad sales
description: At first glance, the quarterly results of Alphabet, the parent company of Google, were not at all bad.Total revenue grew 25% compared to last year, hi
body: At first glance, the quarterly results of Alphabet, the parent company of Google, were not at all bad.Total revenue grew 25% compared to last year, hitting $127.6bn. It was buoyed by the ongoing success of Google Cloud, where revenue grew by 103% to almost $31bn.However, profits at the company fell by a considerable 25% during the quarter. And for the second time in its history as a public company, it showed negative free cash flow, this time in excess of $9bn. That's almost twice the loss of cash Alphabet showed just three months ago.Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments, meaning Alphabet is now spending more money than it is bringing in. That new level of spending is almost entirely dedicated to Google's AI investments.By the end of Thursday,  the company's total stock market value had fallen to $3.46 trillion from $3.97 trillion the day before.Google's omnipresent search engine now defaults to AI summaries of a person's query, and that hit the number of advertisements it was able to sell during the quarter. The sale of ads that appear alongside Google Search results is the vast majority of Alphabet's business.Tracy Woo, a principal analyst at Forrester, said Alphabet's disappointing search business results "highlights the challenge of funding massive AI investments while maintaining the strength of established businesses."Although Phillip Schindler, Google's chief business officer, said on Wednesday that he felt "very good about our trajectory" with an AI-focused version of the search engine, the company's stock fell by almost 13% on Thursday, its second lowest showing this year.Amazon's stock also took a hit on Thursday after it shared results that disappointed investors. Shares of the company fell 6% in after hours stock trading.Alongside quarterly sales growth of 11%, hitting $201bn, the company shared a staggering cash flow figure of negative $42bn.That number shows that Amazon is not only spending more money than it makes, but that spending has increased six-fold over the span of three months.Chief executive Andy Jassy claimed the business was spending in part because it had the chance at, not one, but two businesses that could end up bringing in $1 trillion for Amazon the future.Jassy did not specify what two Amazon businesses those may be. But during a call with financial analysts he repeatedly mentioned the financial opportunity presented by Amazon making and selling its own computer chips, as well as its AI developer platform Bedrock, which offers paying users access to most major AI models and tools."One of the lessons we've learned over 20-plus years is that there is not one tool to rule the world," Jassy said. "People always assume whatever is in the lead early on will be the only thing that people use - it's never true."As Jassy was asked several times to explain the company's spending, he admitted it "would be more convenient" if it were spread over the next 25 years. "That's not the world we live in," he added."We can fund this plan, and I think it will forever change the size, the revenue, the free cash flow of Amazon."Wall Street reacted less enthusiastically to Microsoft's update, with shares falling by less than 1% on Thursday.The company, which is also one of OpenAI's largest investors, spent around $5bn less on investments dedicated to AI. It also revealed earlier this week plans to cut thousands of workers, which will further reduce the company's costs.Meanwhile, its revenue grew 19% from a year earlier, hitting $92.3bn for the quarter. Its crucial cloud business grew by 30% to $63bn.Chief executive Satya Nadella said the use of Copilot, Microsoft's AI chatbot and tool, has seen "automated tasks nearly double since July" as daily users grew by 500% from a year ago.Usually lower spending and growing sales earns a positive reaction from investors.But Woo said Wall Street is trying to look farther into the future when it comes to which businesses will truly make good on their big promises around AI."Microsoft's results reinforce that enterprise demand for AI remains strong, but they also highlight a much bigger question facing the technology industry, where AI value will ultimately be captured," Woo said.

schema.headline: Google value plunges by $500bn as AI search hits ad sales

title: Biggest fibre boost could be scraps in your bin, experts say
description: As a rule of thumb, the skins of fruit and veg pack more fibre than the insides. Eating a kiwi with the skin on, external provides 50% more fibre than
body: As a rule of thumb, the skins of fruit and veg pack more fibre than the insides. Eating a kiwi with the skin on, external provides 50% more fibre than having a peeled one, for example. For their study, the scientists at King's College London analysed 12 raw or uncooked fresh foods - beetroot, bell pepper, broccoli, butternut squash, cauliflower, celeriac, curly kale, fennel, kiwi fruit, leek, pineapple and watermelon. They found many discarded parts contained more fibre than the sections people typically eat.For example:watermelon rind contained 2.10g of fibre per 100g – roughly equivalent to the fibre in a slice of wholemeal breadbutternut squash skin and seeds contained 9.25g per 100g – nearly as much fibre as a bowl of bran flakespineapple skin and core contained five times more fibre than the fleshbroccoli stalks contained fibre, although a bit less than the floretsFibre is essential for your gut to work properly and helps prevent constipation.Project lead Dr Rachel Gibson said the findings suggested people are throwing away a significant amount of fibre."This isn't just a nutritional loss, it's also a financial one - you're effectively throwing away a substantial portion of what you've paid for."King's College London has been experimenting in its canteen, external, offering staff and students root-to-tip meals, such as banana skin curry. At home, people might want to try leaving skins on kiwi fruit, using broccoli stalks in stir-fries or adding bell pepper seeds to dishes, the researchers suggest. While cooking can change the fibre content, it doesn't usually destroy it all.Steaming, microwaving or quick sautéing tends to preserve nutrients best.Gibson said: "This isn't about perfection and this isn't about forcing people to eat unpalatable food – it's about recognising the nutritional value in components we've been conditioned to discard."She acknowledges some may be hesitant to try it. Some diners raised concerns during the canteen trial. Over the nine-week period, "root-to-tip" dishes made up a third of total daily hot menu sales at the university. Those choosing the new dishes were less likely to finish their meals than diners eating from the conventional menu.Kirsten Jackson, a dietitian with the British Dietetic Association who specialises in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), says the food hacks are useful as long as produce is washed thoroughly.She suggests blending pineapple cores into smoothies, but says the tough skins are not something she would recommend.Some stalks may need to be cooked or finely chopped to make them more palatable, she adds."Just because a broccoli stalk doesn't fit into tonight's meal doesn't mean it needs to go in the bin. Chop it up, freeze it and add it to a soup or stir-fry another day," she said.She advises increasing fibre intake gradually to avoid bloating, noting that people who have IBS may find it harder to tolerate.And there are some things to avoid entirely, said the British Nutrition Foundation. Green potatoes and rhubarb leaves contain toxic compounds, while tough stalks and seeds may not be suitable for young children.

schema.headline: Biggest fibre boost could be scraps in your bin, experts say

title: Foreign defence contractors will need to invest in UK under new rules
description: Foreign firms awarded large defence contracts will need to invest an equal value back into the UK to create "bang for the British buck", Defence Secre
body: Foreign firms awarded large defence contracts will need to invest an equal value back into the UK to create "bang for the British buck", Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has announced.Under the new rules, companies receiving more than £50m will need to spend an equivalent amount on British factories, jobs and training.It comes as the government continues to face pressure to hit its target of spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, an objective some opposition MPs and defence analysts have questioned its ability to deliver.Streeting told BBC Breakfast the new rules would help achieve this target given it "does come at a cost to the country and other things we'd like to spend money on"."What we're aiming to do is on the most valuable of those contracts worth £50m or more, is to try and get benefit for Britain, bang for the British buck back here at home," he added.The investment stipulations for foreign businesses, which the government described as its "offset strategy", are hoped to increase investment in Britain's defence industry. The Ministry of Defence will apply the rules on a "case-by-case" basis from April 2027, the government said in a statement.Countries, including Poland, Norway and the Netherlands, have mandated similar rules to "boost the economic benefit from defence procurement", the statement continued.It added: "The government is prioritising buying British defence contracts wherever possible. "Where it must buy defence equipment from overseas, this new approach will ensure British workers and businesses still benefit."Streeting and Chancellor John Healey will unveil the new rules on a visit to the UK defence contractor BAE's shipbuilding site in Glasgow.The policy appears designed to make the proposed extra investment in defence more politically palatable, rather than committing to outright increased direct cuts and spending.It comes as a row continues over how the government will reach its defence spending targets amid tight public finances.Tan Dhesi, Labour chair of the Commons defence select Committee, said key decisions had been "lamentably delayed" to next year's spending review rather than being announced in Wednesday's Budget."We need to urgently rebuild our capabilities now, or we risk leaving ourselves seriously vulnerable in the event of a major conflict," the MP said.And Tory leader Kemi Badenoch said on Wednesday that Healey "failed his own test" by not setting out a "plan for 3%" in the Budget.Streeting has hit back at the criticism, saying he "strongly disagrees" with Dhesi, insisting that the government was not "kicking the can down" the road on defence, as it critics claim. "I think we're doing as much as we can, as fast as we can... of course there is more to do," he told BBC Breakfast.He said delaying detail about hitting the 3% target to next year's spending review was "the right thing to do" so that ministers can look at "spending in the round".He added that the UK was ready to deal with hostile threats, but "we're not where we'd want to be"."There's no sugarcoating the fact that our Armed Forces were under-invested in for more than a decade," he told Breakfast.Some estimates have suggested the government will need to spend an additional  £10bn annually to reach its 3% target by the end of the decade, and match the Nato-wide commitment of spending 3.5% of national income by 2035.Healey resigned as Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary in June, claiming at the time that the former prime minister's proposed defence investment fell "well short of what is required for defence and the country at this dangerous time".

schema.headline: Foreign defence contractors will need to invest in UK under new rules

title: Yorkshire Water chief Nicola Shaw resigns after firm downgraded
description: Yorkshire Water's chief executive has announced she is to step down, just 24 hours after the company was given the lowest possible environmental ratin
body: Yorkshire Water's chief executive has announced she is to step down, just 24 hours after the company was given the lowest possible environmental rating by the Environment AgencyNicola Shaw, who has led the firm since 2022, will leave the role on 1 January to be replaced by Nicola Medalova, a chartered environmental health officer who previously worked for the National Grid.In a statement on Friday, Shaw said it had been a "privilege" to lead the company but that it was "the right time" to leave her post. Shaw has faced criticism in recent years, including for taking £1.3m in undisclosed payments between 2023 and 2025, while the company has come under scrutiny for its performance. On Thursday, the Environment Agency gave the firm one star out of four - its lowest possible rating - meaning Yorkshire Water was classed as a "poorly performing company". The EA said Yorkshire Water was responsible for 260 pollution incidents in 2025, which was its highest total since 2011. In 2024, Ofwat announced it was fining the company £47m for historic sewage leaks.

schema.headline: Yorkshire Water chief Nicola Shaw resigns after firm downgraded

title: From Levi's to Primark - the fashion chains selling mended clothes
description: Toast's repair services are free, but off-the-peg "renewed" pieces fetch higher prices than the originals to reflect their unique character.Levi's, wh
body: Toast's repair services are free, but off-the-peg "renewed" pieces fetch higher prices than the originals to reflect their unique character.Levi's, which boasts probably the longest tradition of being fixed up by its fans using anything from rhinestones to fringed cuffs, is rolling out a workshop programme this year.The firm says its research shows younger customers in particular want to repair more but don't know how. For now, Levi's' workshops focus on traditional mending skills, such as sewing on a button and hemming, rather than visible mends, and at a recent launch event in London, that seemed to be what its Gen Z participants were looking for."I'm from East London. If you have holes in your clothes people are like 'Ha ha! You're poor!'," says 16-year-old school student Bianca.Theo, 19, says he'd rather learn how to mend without it showing."I would want [the jeans] to look how I originally bought them," he says. He has a side hustle selling clothes at car boot sales and thinks traditional repair skills would make it more lucrative.His friend Nicholas, also 19, says most people want to look "fresh"."No-one wants to look like they came out of a dumpster," he says. Still, Paul Dillinger, Levi's head of global design innovation, thinks more creative repairs will win them over as they pick up more skills."No-one has time for that perfect 'straight from the shop' thing. That's not cool. "People crave agency," he says. "Mending is a demonstration of humanity: it's not a mustard stain, it's a memory of a great day in the ballpark."

schema.headline: From Levi's to Primark - the fashion chains selling mended clothes

title: Gareth Ward defends Michelin-star Ynyshir after food hygeine debacle
description: The chef at Wales' only two-Michelin-star restaurant has defended the way he operates his kitchen after the venue came under scrutiny over food hygien
body: The chef at Wales' only two-Michelin-star restaurant has defended the way he operates his kitchen after the venue came under scrutiny over food hygiene standards.While chasing a third Michelin star, Ynyshir was handed a one-star hygiene rating in February and told to improve due to concerns about raw and undercooked foods.The news made global headlines and was a blow to Ward and his team, but in Apple TV's documentary series Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars, Ward said Ynyshir was "an incredible place"."There's nothing in there that's amateurish," he told the programme. "I run a spotless kitchen."Ward, who co-owns the restaurant near Machynlleth in mid Wales, added the hygiene rating had hurt, "because we are only trying to be the best"."Whether you're a cafe, or a pub, or a two-Michelin-star restaurant. We've all got the same rules," he told the eight-part second series of the show, which follows elite chefs and their teams."But we go above and beyond everything to make what we do safe."Ynyshir was previously ordered to stop serving raw lobster after Ceredigion council found "significant hazards" were not properly identified.The restaurant received its first Michelin star in 2014 and its second in 2022, becoming the first and only restaurant in Wales to hold two. It missed out on a third star at the ceremony this year.The 16-seat restaurant serves Japanese-inspired raw dishes as part of its nearly £500 a head 30-course tasting menu, and accused inspectors of not understanding its specialised procedures.By August, the council had reinstated its five-star hygiene rating after it found the "business had addressed all matters identified during the original inspection".But, for Ynyshir, the scrutiny was a major setback, and Ward shared his frustration in the documentary."I'm very proud of my whole team and my business, and what we've achieved," he said."It's obviously massive in the media, which anyone instantly jumps on and thinks it's about cleanliness," he said. "I run a spotless kitchen."When something like this happens you're a bit blown away."Ward said the restaurant served a lot of raw food and did a lot of things "that aren't normal"."We have done some things wrong, but we don't deserve everything [we were accused of]," he said."It's just, we dare to be different."He said the inspection left him feeling the weight of responsibility, with more than 30 members of staff and the business potentially at risk.Management of food safety at Ynyshir was categorised by inspectors as needing major improvement, as was cleanliness and condition of facilities, while "hygienic food handling" was rated "generally satisfactory".A dirty floor, inadequate hand-washing facilities in some areas and broken equipment posing a potential contamination risk were also identified in the inspectors' report.Ynyshir responded at the time, saying the inspection "identified a small number of minor issues typical of a busy professional kitchen situated in the countryside of rural Wales" which had been "rectified immediately and in full".It said biological testing, at "significant cost" to the restaurant, had "conclusively confirmed that our techniques are safe, compliant and appropriate".It said at the time it was prepared to work constructively with the council but expected "an informed, consistent and fair assessment process that recognises the realities of modern, non-conventional restaurants".When Ynyshir was reinspected, Ceredigion council said the "business had addressed all matters identified during the original inspection".

schema.headline: Gareth Ward defends Michelin-star Ynyshir after food hygeine debacle

title: Syrians grow frustrated as soaring living costs threaten recovery
description: Last month, protests erupted in squares and streets across Syria. People burned tyres, blocked roads and chanted slogans, angry at the government's de
body: Last month, protests erupted in squares and streets across Syria. People burned tyres, blocked roads and chanted slogans, angry at the government's decision to raise fuel prices again. It was the largest show of discontent yet since President Ahmed al-Sharaa came to power two years ago. Speaking on a Syrian TV channel, a man said he still supported the authorities but that his situation had deteriorated to the point where he could no longer afford to buy bread. "Honestly," another said, "we have begun to fear what kind of new decision each morning will bring".The increase was the latest in a series of measures people blame for a growing cost-of-living crisis. For many Syrians, life, financially, has worsened since rebels led by Sharaa ousted President Bashar al-Assad, ending five decades of his family's brutal rule and more than 13 years of a devastating civil war. Catapulted to the presidency, Sharaa has, since then, led Syria's transition and efforts to revive a broken economy after a long period of mismanagement, isolation and conflict.There was never any doubt about how challenging this would be. But as they celebrated Assad's overthrow and their new freedoms, Syrians, perhaps unrealistically, hoped things would quickly improve. That, however, has not materialised, and the handling of the economy has frustrated many here.From essential bills to basic items, the cost of virtually everything has gone up. And many saw a further and unexpected rise in fuel prices as a sign of a government out of touch with its country. "We don't want roundabouts. Every day they build a new roundabout. People stood by you and are still with you," another protester said, addressing Sharaa, "but this will [make] things explode".Days later, amid calls for further demonstrations, the increase was revoked.In a suburb of Damascus, I joined Fatima Saleh Eid at an open-air market for her weekly shop. At 50, she works as a cleaner to help support her family. "We've suffered a lot," she said. Her husband had recently been hired by a ceramic factory after a year unemployed. He is among the lucky ones, as many are struggling to find work. In some streets, men gather in the hope of meeting someone offering a day job; often, they wait in vain.Since coming to power, the government has slashed long-held subsidies as part of an austerity drive. The price of bread, a Syrian staple, has increased tenfold. Fuel prices are now in line with the international average, which has put pressure on farmers and made transportation more expensive, while the cost of electricity has gone up several hundred per cent for some. The authorities, in response, have adjusted public sector wages, including pensions; unsurprisingly, the effect of the additional pay for people has been lost as prices keep rising."We eat more sparingly now. We can't afford chicken anymore nor meat. We only eat vegetables but even [that is] expensive," Fatima said. "Inshallah [God willing] things will get cheaper."As she spoke, around a dozen people, of all ages, gathered around us. Nobody disagreed. One elderly man also said he had stopped eating meat. Another, in his 20s, told me his family were no longer able to pay the medicine for his father, who had a heart condition. One young woman said she and her four children could only afford to have a proper meal every two days.Marwan Bashour, a 68-year-old pensioner, said his monthly pay was around $90 (£70), which is the public sector minimum wage. "It's not enough at all," he said. The United Nations Development Programme said 90% of Syrians were in poverty last year. Marwan told me how he made ends meet. "Sometimes I borrow money, sometimes I sell things from my house," he said, "like an old pot or plates that we never used, gifts that were given to us. I've even had to sell furniture".There have been other pressures too. Like many Syrians, Marwan used to rely on help from aid agencies. But, for him, that has stopped, as organisations have been forced to cut back services because of funding cuts. Sharaa has, of course, scored some important gains. International sanctions imposed in the Assad-era have been lifted, and the US has removed the country from its list of state sponsors of terrorism. Security remains volatile and a source of concern, but the country feels more stable. And the president continues to consolidate his power and, earlier this year, retook the resource-rich north-east from a Kurdish-led militia. (The Druze still control areas in the south, where they want to create an autonomous state; Israel occupies parts of the south-west.)But real economic recovery is yet to happen. Large parts of Syria remain in ruins after a war that killed half a million people and displaced half of the population. Unable to afford rent, many families live in partially destroyed buildings. The World Bank says reconstruction costs are estimated at $216bn and, without foreign help and investment, it will be impossible for Syrians to rebuild.Samir Aita, a Syrian economist who heads the Circle of Arab Economists, a Paris-based independent think-tank, said the crisis was a "combination of policies with the [government] not managing expectations and creating unrealistic hopes". When I asked him about how he felt about the future, he said: "It's unsustainable. If they don't change, I fear chaos."Exhausted after years of conflict, Syrians, left with almost no choice, remain hopeful. Abu Mahmoud, a cab driver, told me: "They inherited the country bankrupt, so people need to be patient. Things don't happen overnight."Additional reporting by Lana Antaki, Samantha Granville and Neha Sharma

schema.headline: Syrians grow frustrated as soaring living costs threaten recovery

title: Newspaper headlines: 'No welfare cuts' and 'Police probe Epstein's stay at Balmoral'
description: The Daily Express, external reports that police are looking into the time spent in Scotland by Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell, hosted by Andrew
body: The Daily Express, external reports that police are looking into the time spent in Scotland by Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell, hosted by Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor. The paper says officers are probing the late sex offender's stay at Balmoral, believed to be in 1999. Police Scotland tells the Express it has "received information" and inquiries are ongoing. The former prince has always strenuously denied wrongdoing.The Times, external says former prime minister Gordon Brown is helping the government draw up plans to boost defence funding, in such a way that avoids having to raise taxes, or cut public spending. Ministers are said to be in talks with several Nato countries about setting up an international bank, whose financing would not count as new borrowing.'Humiliation for Healey' is the Daily Mail's, external headline. The paper says Chancellor John Healey was forced into a climbdown, after appearing to suggest on BBC Radio 4's Today programme that the welfare bill would be cut before the next election. The paper says his comments triggered chaos in Whitehall, with Downing Street later saying it was "not setting an arbitrary target or timetable".Stills from a video showing Healey downing a pint in the pub, after Wednesday's Budget, appear across the papers. On the front of the Daily Telegraph, external the chancellor can be seen with his red tie flung over his shoulder holding the empty glass upside-down above his head. A campaign group tells the paper the move was 'tone deaf' given the inflation-linked rise in beer duty, announced by Healey, hours earlier. The Times, external sketch writer Tom Peck runs the numbers and writes that the chancellor consumed the equivalent of 6.5% of the government's £100 energy rebate – in 12.4 seconds.Sir Patrick Stewart is pictured on many of the front pages after the actor's death at the age of 86. 'A Yorkshire lad who reached for the stars' is the Daily Mirror's, external headline. The Guardian, external remembers Sir Patrick's "even-keeled performance" on the bridge of the Starship Enterprise and his "steely directives" of "engage" and "make it so", which turned him into a global star.

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'No welfare cuts' and 'Police probe Epstein's stay at Balmoral'

title: Serbia: Student-backed election winners demand sweeping resignations
description: Serbia's victorious student-led movement has called for top figures in the police, intelligence and judiciary to stand down, days after ousting ex-pre
body: Serbia's victorious student-led movement has called for top figures in the police, intelligence and judiciary to stand down, days after ousting ex-president Aleksandar Vučić's party from power.Standing in Pioneers' Park opposite parliament, newly elected MPs on the Student List demanded the immediate dismissal of all police officers who had broken the law, singling out the heads of the police, the BIA security agency and anti-terror unit.It is not often a European country votes to fully reset its political system overnight, and Serbians have voted to hand the task to a group of novice politicians, made up of intellectuals, professors, artists, athletes and as many as 12 medical doctors and surgeons.But the handover of power will take weeks, and the students' movement is concerned that evidence of possible wrongdoing could be destroyed in that time.Just a few days ago, the park they were standing in on Thursday was a tent camp, filled with Vučić loyalists outside his office.Within hours of him admitting defeat on Sunday night, the camp was dismantled, and a team of volunteers moved in on Monday morning to clean up the mess.They have made some bold promises. Under their Student Plan, they promise to "halt the plunder, return stolen goods to the state budget, and invest directly in education and the economy".The purge of Vučić loyalists has already begun at Serbia's state broadcaster RTS, where director Manja Grčić has stepped down. Newly elected MP Mirjana Nikolić said Serbian citizens had the right to truthful information and RTS had served the interests of the government for years.The new MPs have also set their sights on replacing the head of Telekom Srbija, Vladimir Lučić.Vučić loyalist Ana Brnabić, who is currently Serbia's acting president, has accused her opponents of choosing "revolutionary justice, not rule of law," and of aiming to shut down "all of the media they dislike".But one of the next government's best-known MPs, Dejan Šoškić, argues that key reforms need to be in place fast."In the first six months, I would like to see the media scene liberated, fighting against corruption on the way, the institutions operating as prescribed by laws and a lustration law introduced," said Šoškić, an economist who served as governor of the central bank between 2010 and 2012.By lustration, he means banning from public office members of the Vučić government or party apparatus who are found to have violated the rights of Serbians.That kind of purge will take time, as all of Serbia's main pillars of authority have been held by Vučić and his party for so long, warns Strahinja Subotić of Belgrade-based European Policy Centre.Ultimately, he believes the new administration will have to "build bridges to the segments that have been operating well in the past".All 141 successful candidates were chosen by students from universities across Serbia through a lengthy, secretive and carefully crafted process, and tasked with implementing the movement's plan for a complete rebuild of the country.That political agenda took months for a highly diverse group of students to agree to. Now it is up to the equally disparate team of successful candidates to put the plan into practice, rather than the students themselves.Another prominent figure on the Student List, is Radomir Saičić, a professor of organic chemistry at the University of Belgrade."While the practical mechanisms will be developed on the go, the new MPs will stick to the students' 1200-page long and detailed plan," he told the BBC."Parliament is making decisions, but since this change was led by students' efforts, we would highly value their opinion and work closely with them," he promised.Not only are they newcomers to politics, but Serbia's election winners have no obvious leader and are faced with a series of complex challenges, including taking on the country's highly complex balancing act on the international stage.Serbia is both a candidate to join the European Union and maintains close relations with Russia. Its bid to join the bloc has long been on the back-burner, while its Western Balkan neighbours press ahead.The EU was quick to welcome the Student List victory and has promised to back their push for reforms to the rule of law, media freedom and fight against corruption.But EU integration occupies a strikingly minor place in the students' election manifesto, which describes the bloc merely as Serbia's "most important economic partner".For years, Belgrade has balanced its foreign policy between the EU and its eastern partners, Russia and China. Belgrade has managed to stand out in Europe by not imposing sanctions on Moscow since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.In return, Serbia has been rewarded with preferential gas prices that have helped maintain domestic stability, and Vladimir Putin publicly endorsed Vučić's bid to remain in power.That does not mean that the students have any plans to change course, and changing Serbia's foreign policy may not be high on their list."Serbia had it own experience with sanctions in the 1990s and we know that they mostly harm ordinary people and do not affect policies of a state," said Dejan Šoškić, referring to UN sanctions imposed during the wars in former Yugoslavia.The new government's initial focus will most likely be on domestic reform, and the clock is already ticking before the next election campaign, with presidential elections due to take place in December.Aleksandar Vučić is legally barred from running for a third term as president, but he has promised that his defeated Serbian Progressive Party will fight back: "We will beat them much faster than they can even imagine."

schema.headline: Serbia: Student-backed election winners demand sweeping resignations

title: Lewis Hamilton says F1 has 'never had anyone like me' as Ferrari driver vows before Mexico Grand Prix to keep racing until sport returns to Africa
description: Lewis Hamilton says he is unlike any driver Formula 1 has seen before and reaffirmed a determination to keep racing into his mid-forties.The seven-tim
body: Lewis Hamilton says he is unlike any driver Formula 1 has seen before and reaffirmed a determination to keep racing into his mid-forties.The seven-time world champion recently said he wanted to continue in the sport to fulfil a dream of racing in Africa, having campaigned for a Grand Prix there for many years.F1 has signed a 10-year deal with the central-east African country of Rwanda starting in the early 2030s which will be a first race on the continent since 1993.The Briton said F1 had "never had anyone like me in the 70 years" of the sport and he felt like he was "built differently".Hamilton will be at least 45 when that race takes place - the same age as Aston Martin driver Fernando Alonso, who is continuing in F1 next year - but he told a news conference before this weekend's Mexico Grand Prix that he should be considered a special case."Of course there are challenges up ahead that I can't foresee that come with age. But along this journey there have been so many pre-conceived ideas like that your reaction time drops off," he said."Did you see my reaction time in the last race? It was faster than some of the youngest people here."As long as you are willing to sacrifice everything, which I am right now – I can't say in four years whether I will want to continue doing what I'm doing – but I am still all in. I will be for the foreseeable future."

schema.headline: Lewis Hamilton says F1 has 'never had anyone like me' as Ferrari driver vows before Mexico Grand Prix to keep racing until sport returns to Africa

title: 'Respected and beloved': Tributes pour in for Sir Patrick Stewart
description: Sir Ian McKellen leads tributes to 'beloved actor' Sir Patrick Stewart after his death at 86Figure caption, Watch: The life of legendary actor Sir Pat
body: Sir Ian McKellen leads tributes to 'beloved actor' Sir Patrick Stewart after his death at 86Figure caption, Watch: The life of legendary actor Sir Patrick StewartByJamie Whitehead and Harry SekulichUpdated 1 hour agoSir Ian McKellen has led tributes to Sir Patrick Stewart following his death at the age of 86, calling him "the most respected and beloved actor of his generation".Tributes to the renowned British actor have poured in since his death at his Los Angeles home after "a brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy Body Dementia was announced on Thursday."He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and, in my case, love," Sir Ian, Sir Patrick's X-Men co-star, said.Famous for his role as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek, Sir Patrick was a versatile actor who won multiple awards, balancing Hollywood roles and a career in classical theatre.William Shatner, who also helmed the USS Enterprise in Star Trek, said Sir Patrick brought "intelligence, grace and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did"."Captain Picard stood for the best of us and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work," Shatner added.Stewart depicted Picard in more than 170 episodes of the hit sci-fi TV series between 1987 and 1994, as well as in four feature films. He returned to the role for Star Trek: Picard in 2020.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, William Shatner (right) said Sir Patrick "stood for the best of us"George Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu in Star Trek, said the actor "inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity".Sir Patrick would later be celebrated for his portrayal of Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men film franchise.Hugh Jackman, who starred alongside him in the franchise, called him a "tremendous friend and man", saying: "We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today."Sir Ian, a longtime friend of his X-Men co-star, who officiated his wedding in 2013, said Sir Patrick was "defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire"."You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues."Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, Sir Ian McKellen and Sir Patrick Stewart alongside their younger X-Men replacements at the X-Men: Days of Future Past premiereSir Ian recalled first meeting Sir Patrick as young actors in the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC) and how he had expressed caution over him taking on the Star Trek role."He took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did," said Sir Ian, who appeared with Sir Patrick in a 2009 theatre production of Waiting for Godot.He added that while the US had become Sir Patrick's "adopted home", he "never forsook his origins" growing up in Yorkshire, and said "the proudest achievement of the most respected and beloved actor of his generation on either side of the Atlantic, was his appointment as chancellor of Huddersfield University".Sir Ian noted that Sir Patrick's final film appearance will be as Professor X in the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday film. Marvel Studios described him as "a singular talent, a generous collaborator and a true gentleman".Sir Patrick died on Wednesday "in the loving care of his wife", a statement from his family said. "We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace," it added.The veteran actor is survived by his wife, Sunny Ozell, as well as by his two adult children from his first marriage, Daniel and Sophie Stewart.Figure caption, Watch: "A big loss" - Fans react to death of Sir Patrick StewartBorn in the town of Mirfield in 1940, Sir Patrick's love of drama began at school where he was introduced to Shakespeare and his first public performance was in a local church production of Cinderella.He threw himself enthusiastically into the flourishing local theatre. "I used to recite Shakespeare from memory," he said. "I just learned all these big speeches."When Sir Patrick was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010, he said he owed "literally everything" to his former English teacher who first encouraged him to perform. His first foray into professional acting was when he joined the RSC in 1966, going on to play King John, Oberon in A Midsummer Night's Dream and Henry IV.The RSC described him as a "colossus of both stage and screen", remembering him as "one of the finest classical Shakespearean actors of his generation" whose contribution to the company was "beyond measure".Image source, ReutersImage caption, His third wife, Sunny Ozell, was with the actor when he passed awayDame Harriet Walter, who first met Sir Patrick in his theatre days more than 40 years ago, said his passing was like a "huge giant tree has fallen in the forest"."He had fire in his eyes and you were absolutely in the room with him," the Succession actress told BBC Newsnight. "I've never heard a bad word against him. And I think the world's going to be very poor without him."As well as having roles in films such as Safe House, Robin Hood: Men in Tights and the original Dune, Sir Patrick continued to appear on TV throughout his career, making guest appearances on Frasier, Futurama and Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt.US actor and animator Seth MacFarlane, who grew up as a fan of Sir Patrick, said he was "gifted the privilege of becoming a colleague and friend" as they worked together on Family Guy, American Dad! and Ted. MacFarlane described him as a "rare actor who could take any bit of dialogue and elevate it, making a good writer sound great and a great writer sound masterful".Image caption, Appearing in the BBC programme Extras in 2005 Comedian Ricky Gervais, whose BBC programme Extras Sir Patrick guest starred in, described him as a "legend".Sharing a video of the pair giggling in a set of bloopers for the series, Gervais said: "I still can't believe he agreed to do this scene. And he didn't even mind when I ruined every take."Sir Patrick was a lifelong supporter of English Football League club Huddersfield Town, which called him a "titan of his craft"."Fiercely proud of his Yorkshire roots, Sir Patrick was a Terrier in every sense, and we're proud to have counted him as one of our own," the club added.Alzheimer's is the most common type of dementia, while Lewy Body Dementia is another common form caused by abnormal protein deposits, which cause a loss of cognitive function.The Alzheimer's Society CEO Michelle Dyson said Sir Patrick was an "extraordinarily talented and much-loved actor, admired by millions around the world", adding: "His death is a heartbreaking reminder of the devastating impact dementia has on people and families across the globe."

schema.headline: 'Respected and beloved': Tributes pour in for Sir Patrick Stewart

title: Cubans in Florida waver on Trump and Republicans over immigration
description: Since the Trump administration launched its crackdown on undocumented immigrants two years ago, the waiting room of Cuban-born immigration lawyer, Ism
body: Since the Trump administration launched its crackdown on undocumented immigrants two years ago, the waiting room of Cuban-born immigration lawyer, Ismael Labrador, in Miami is never empty. His appointment book is packed with relatives of detained immigrants trying to secure their release before they're deported back to their countries of origin.Although business is booming, Labrador wishes it wasn't."We have relatives living in fear right now, we've had relatives who have been deported back to Cuba, unfortunately," he explains.Cubans have traditionally enjoyed favoured immigration status in the United States under provisions enshrined in 1960s-era legislation called the Cuban Adjustment Act. But widespread arrests across Florida by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents have left the Cuban American community more vulnerable in the US than they'd ever imagined, says Labrador."The way I put it is that if you don't have a Green Card in the United States, you may be a target."Five ways Trump has changed immigration in the USCountless mobile phone videos have recorded such arrests in places previously considered off-limits: parents detained outside schoolyards, at bus stops, youth sporting events and even inside courthouses at pre-arranged immigration hearings.Few have had the impact of the footage of 39-year-old Ecuadorean immigrant, Grace Calero, and her 19-year-old daughter, Giulianna Carriel, being arrested in a hospital ward.Two months ago, the pair were driving to work in Kissimmee, central Florida when they were hit by another car and taken to hospital in an ambulance. While they were being treated for their injuries, ICE agents burst in and arrested them. They were deported back to Ecuador within days.Labrador's cousin has also been caught up in the dragnet of ICE detentions. Despite his best efforts, the immigration lawyer was unable to prevent his own relative from being deported back to Cuba."It's hard when you're fighting against a lot of resources," he laments.The Trump administration has repeatedly said the president was elected on a promise to deliver mass deportations and is delivering on that. "He stopped the invasion of our country and as a result of his policies more than 3 million illegal aliens have left the US," a White House spokeswoman told the BBC last week.ICE, meanwhile, has said it is targeting anyone who has broken American immigration law and is in the country illegally.GUIDE: What are the US midterms?IN DEPTH: The real reasons there are so few young US politicians EXPLORE: Where the US midterms will be won and lostVERIFY: How the US economy is really doing under TrumpNEWSLETTER: Sign up for Anthony Zurcher's analysis in your inboxLabrador was among the 68% of Cuban Americans in Florida who voted for Donald Trump two years ago, a decision he roundly regrets today.Few could accuse Trump of hiding his plans on immigration. On the campaign trail in 2024, he touted his policy of mass deportations of undocumented migrants."On Day One, I will launch the largest deportation programme in American history", he said repeatedly at rallies, including in Florida.How Trump’s Cuba policy is shaping Miami’s midtermsLabrador – and many thousands of disillusioned Latino voters like him – thought the administration would only deport people with criminal records."I think we got blindsided by the administration," he argues."Personally, I voted for Trump because I wanted to get criminals out of the country," he says, alleging that "communists came in from Cuba under Biden.""We wanted to have a safe America. We never thought that he was going to go after everybody.""This isn't what I voted for," he insists.Labrador is far from the only Cuban American in Florida to experience buyer's remorse over President Trump.Congresswoman Maria Elvira Salazar, who represents Florida's 27th Congressional district, recently released a video filmed outside the White House in which she distanced herself from his deportation policy saying it had gone "too far"."The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today," she said, addressing President Trump. Salazar is locked in a tight race against another Cuban American, the Democratic Party's candidate, Eliott Rodríguez. Her close association with Trump on immigration could potentially cost Salazar her congressional seat.Florida remains a Trump stronghold. At a recent gathering of Cuban American entrepreneurs in Miami, the atmosphere remained staunchly pro-Trump. "Miami loves Trump, Cuban Americans love Trump," says real estate businessman, Juan Omar Sixto, motioning at the other guests behind him."They agree with Trump that anyone who crossed the border illegally should be out," he says, despite acknowledging he illegally entered the US himself six decades earlier.A poll released on Thursday, external by Florida International University found that not all South Florida Cubans agree - 76% said they disapprove of the Trump administration's deportations of Cubans with no criminal record. But their support for the Republican Party remains steadfast, with 68% saying they plan to vote Republican in November. In other parts of the country, support amongst Latinos is declining.In the last election, Trump beat Kamala Harris by 56.1% to 43% - the biggest margin of victory for a candidate in the state since 1988 - in part because of the support of Latino communities. But a recent NBC News/Telemundo poll of 8,000 registered Latino voters showed nearly 60% favour seeing Congress come under Democratic Party control to just 35% wanting a Republican victory.The high cost of living is a big factor for people's discontent, as residents feel supermarket and petrol prices are impossibly high for working families.But for many Hispanics, it's also partly because of stories like Heydi Sanchez's.Sanchez left Cuba in 2019 as the island spiralled into economic collapse and illegally crossed the border from Mexico into the US. After nine months in a detention centre, she was released under an i-220B Order of Supervision which grants the right to remain in the US but carries the constant threat of deportation.Sanchez settled in Tampa where she worked with autistic children and the elderly. After a complex and expensive fertility struggle, she and her husband had a baby girl called Kailyn.Most i-220B holders try to normalise their immigration status via 'humanitarian parole' and must check in with ICE agents at regular scheduled appointments. Last year, President Trump revoked temporary humanitarian parole to about 300,000 Cubans. Sanchez knew something was wrong in her case when her regular ICE meeting was brought forward without warning.At the appointment, she was detained. Kailyn was taken from her arms and passed to her father, a US citizen. Within a day, Sanchez was on a deportation flight back to Havana in shackles with no recourse to appeal.I met her in Cuba where she now lives in a one-bed apartment in Mayabeque, a rural province outside Havana."It's like the sky fell in and crushed me", she says of being separated from her daughter."When we have video calls, she says: 'Mummy, come home.' And I say: 'darling, Mummy is away working.' What else can I tell her? How can I explain it?'", Sanchez asks, unable to hold back the tears.Despite expressions of support from several US politicians, including Maria Elvira Salazar, more than a year has passed since her deportation and Sanchez remains in limbo in Cuba.In a statement, ICE said that "in this case, the parent stated they wanted to be removed without the child and left the child in the care of a safe relative in the United States".While the Trump Administration has rolled back Cubans' special immigration privileges, it has sent thousands of people back to an island Washington itself describes as a "failed state". Cuba is in the grip of its worst ever energy crisis amid a months-long fuel blockade imposed by the US.Since overwhelmingly voting for Trump in 2024, Cubans in Florida now realise they are just as vulnerable to deportation as any other diaspora. His Republican colleagues may feel the brunt of their frustration at the ballot box.

schema.headline: Cubans in Florida waver on Trump and Republicans over immigration

title: We went on holiday with our neighbours and swapped families - it tore us apart
description: Image source, Rachel StoneImage caption, Rachel as a baby with her father Rex and brother Ian - and Rachel todayByEmily DoughtyUpdated 4 hours agoRach
body: Image source, Rachel StoneImage caption, Rachel as a baby with her father Rex and brother Ian - and Rachel todayByEmily DoughtyUpdated 4 hours agoRachel Stone was five and her brother Ian was 10 when their mum and dad took them on a caravan holiday to Wales with the family next door.They spent two fun-filled weeks together - but when they got home, each family split in half and swapped houses.Rachel and her mother Kay moved in with the neighbour Eddie and his daughter Alison. Eddie's wife Irene and their daughter Dawn moved in with Rachel's dad Rex and her brother Ian.Rachel tells Dr Sian Williams, host of Radio 4's Life Changing podcast, of the trauma of her family being torn apart, the chaos that unfolded and how she has come to forgive her parents.Image source, Rachel StoneImage caption, Rachel's dad Rex and brother Ian remained in their old home, while she moved in next door with her motherRachel and Ian had initially been delighted when a new family moved in next door. "We instantly hit it off, all four of us." They were thrilled to be going on holiday together. Rachel remembers two caravans parked side-by-side and a trip up Mount Snowdon. But when it was time to go home, everything was mixed up - people were getting in the wrong cars.Rachel remembers her mum leaning back from the passenger seat, saying: "'We're going to have a new family. We're going to be living in number eight with Eddie and Alison. Alison's going to be your new sister."And your dad and brother are still going to live in number 10. And Auntie Irene and Dawn are going to live there. And Dawn's going to be your brother's new sister."Rachel immediately felt "very panicked and afraid and upset" and says she started to cry.As the car rumbled along, she felt "bewildered, but also a little bit excited". She liked Alison and had always wanted a sister.That night, Alison let her sleep on her top bunk and the next morning the adults switched belongings between the houses in the Isle of Sheppey where they lived.Rachel says she felt very confused. "You can't help but think that it's your fault."Life ChangingMy family was 'jumbled up'28 October 2026Life at number 8, where Rachel now lived, was very different to number 10. Her old house had been clean, whereas this house had "dog hair, greasy things, car things".She describes her mum as "firm but fair" and very practical.Her stepdad Eddie "was never horrible to me, but I never called him dad. I wasn't his girl."She also missed Ian desperately. "I was very proud of him. He was my big brother."I used to wait in the front garden for him to come home from school when I was a toddler." Image source, Rachel StoneImage caption, Rachel, pictured here at nine years old, says life with her new family at number 8 was very different to her old life Rachel was seven when the two couples went to court together and got divorced. They later married their new partners in separate low-key registry office ceremonies. Rachel did not even know her dad had married Irene until she saw the wedding photo. Her visits to her old home tailed off when she was about 11 or 12. She says she found it difficult to go and visit her dad and did not get along with Irene. Meanwhile, life with her mum Kay and Eddie was chaotic."[He] was quite possessive and controlling. By the time we got to 13, she [Mum] said, 'it's not sustainable, [we] can't live like this".Image source, Rachel StoneImage caption, Rex and Kay on their wedding day. They went on to divorce and marry their neighbours Rachel said school was her "escape". She got good grades and became a teacher. She got married and had two sons but is now separated and works as a business coach.Throughout her life, Rachel's mother would never talk about the swap. "I asked a lot of questions. She told me it was complicated."Decades later, on a family holiday with her own sons, Rachel asked again."I said to my mum, 'Oh, Joseph's 10 now... Ian was 10 when you let him go with Dad and Irene.'"She says her mum was "beside herself with guilt and the shame... for her selfish decisions""Years later she actually said to me - the words I almost wanted to hear all my life  - 'I'm so sorry I let you down and I want to try and make it up to you.'" Rachel says it was the start of her rebuilding a "wonderful" relationship with her mum. Image source, Rachel StoneImage caption, Despite being separated as children, siblings Rachel and Ian remain close Rachel never had a close relationship with her dad. "He told me he had a choice between his wife and his children. Unfortunately for me, he chose his wife."He and Irene stayed together until his death aged 81. But when she spoke at her dad's funeral, Rachel said she felt she owed him an apology."I imagined a character of a perfect dad that had been taken away from me... I created this superhuman being that could be everything."And I wanted him to be like that. But I also think you have to accept people for who they are."I think that parents do the best they can... You can't hope for your parents to be something they're not."Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: We went on holiday with our neighbours and swapped families - it tore us apart

title: I didn't know when I collapsed at work - it was low vitamin D
description: Twenty-three-year-old Saskia Reeves-Priestley was at work when she suddenly collapsed."I just felt really dizzy, really nauseous, was having heart pal
body: Twenty-three-year-old Saskia Reeves-Priestley was at work when she suddenly collapsed."I just felt really dizzy, really nauseous, was having heart palpitations and was really hot," she says.There had been no prior warning. Saskia, a special educational needs teacher, was a keen goalkeeper who played football four times a week and felt fit and healthy.She would later be diagnosed as vitamin D-deficient – blood tests showed her levels were "next to nothing".In the UK, low vitamin rates are increasing in some age groups, external - particularly in girls and young women.According to data from the National Diet and Nutrition Survey, last year nearly a quarter of 11- to 18-year-olds were classed as deficient.Vitamin D can come from our diet, in foods such as oily fish and meat, or supplements. But most is made by our body when UV light in sunlight hits the skin. Lower levels of sunlight - depending on where in the world you live or the time of year - decrease the body's ability to produce it.Covering parts of the body and wearing sunscreen also has an impact - despite their protective advantages.Those with darker skin need exposure to stronger light to produce the same amount of vitamin D as lighter skin.Doctors don't routinely offer blood tests to check for vitamin D deficiency, but will offer a supplement if a patient is concerned they might be high risk.

schema.headline: I didn't know when I collapsed at work - it was low vitamin D

title: Tony Pulis column: Why managers must put their own fitness first
description: I had worked under and alongside managers for my entire working life as a player and then coach, but it was only when I got my first management job -
body: I had worked under and alongside managers for my entire working life as a player and then coach, but it was only when I got my first management job - at Bournemouth in 1992 - that I realised the workload you undertake and just how time consuming and stressful a job it is.In those days, and in fact throughout my whole career, I wanted to be the person who made all the footballing decisions at my club.That meant I did everything from scouting players to signing the ones I wanted, and organised my staff at every level from first-team to the reserve and youth teams, all within the club's financial restraints.I saw the first-team performances as being my main responsibility so I never wavered from my work on the training ground either, coaching a certain way that suited the players and gave them the best chance of winning games - which would ultimately determine my future.All of the above was generally the way most English clubs were run so it was not just me doing it. But the demands were relentless, and I had to learn how to look after myself properly to cope.During those early days, my management of myself personally was really poor.It starts with your diet. At that time I would be driving up and down the motorway to watch players, trying to find a fish and chip shop or fuelled only by a half-time pie or a sandwich from a local shop.I was young and could deal with it, so it never crossed my mind that I wasn't eating well or getting the exercise I needed to retain my own fitness levels.But, at the same time, the pressure on the team to win games ultimately fell on my shoulders so the pressure of being the person responsible for results and performances every week really built up.I had never realised how stressful that part of management was until we started to lose a few games and every bit of criticism was directed on to my lap.That part has not changed for managers now.They may have less to do with the way their clubs are run now but they still have to deal with people they have never met criticising their ability to do a job they love to media outlets, without taking into consideration any other factors that might be contributing to those performances and results.That's why it's so stressful. All the arrows and guns are pointed in your direction, and you have no way of protecting yourself, apart from by winning games.Many a young manager will have experienced these factors, which could and would affect their health and wellbeing.The turning point for me came when I spoke to an Australian triathlete just before I left Bournemouth in 1994.His advice was pretty blunt and straightforward. He told me doing my job was physically hampering my own fitness levels - but more worrying were the stress levels that came with it, because they could have a major effect on my life itself.It was only after having that conversation that I realised the compromises I was making for my career at the cost of my own health.I came to the conclusion that in my next job, if I got one, I would dedicate myself to a more manageable lifestyle and put my own fitness first.I decided I would work out early every morning before breakfast at the club I managed, so I could then dedicate the rest of my day to my work.Yes, there were days I would be empty and would only walk and stretch, but generally I stuck to that rule and worked hard to keep on top of myself physically.At Gillingham in 1999, I decided to run a marathon - my first London Marathon - which got me focused during the season in respect of my physical health.That was my first challenge of many I have taken on for charity down the years. I have also cycled from John O' Groats to Land's End, walked up Mount Kilimanjaro, and rowed from Tower Bridge to the Eiffel Tower.All of this exercise also helped my stress levels, especially in respect of sleeping. Being tired going to bed really helped my sleeping hours and meant I was never kept awake worrying about what was going wrong at work.There were other ways I looked after my mental health too. Even as the internet exploded, I have never read any press, good or bad, about me or my team.I always worked as hard I could at every club I was with, and picked good staff who I was able to confide in, but I was able to switch off too, thanks to my family.I've written in previous columns about my routine after games and how I would often drive home to the south coast on a Saturday night, reflecting on our result and starting my preparation for our next game.But Sundays were always about spending all day with the family.Whether it was watching my son Anthony playing football as a young boy, or just being around the children full stop, that was how I relaxed and that day with them became a release valve which was an important part of my routine.When I speak to young managers now, I give them the same advice I followed.You have to maintain your enthusiasm for looking after yourself, because this is the time when you will need it the most. Under the constant stress you will put yourself under, it is dangerous not to.But, while everyone knows the risks of the job, many are prepared to take them. I always was.Years ago, managers' health was never much of a concern to clubs - we probably drank too much and ate too many of the wrong foods, at all hours of the day and night, but that was just part of the lifestyle that went with it.Now, there is lots more support - the League Managers' Association offers frequent health testing under its 'Fit To Manage' programme, and most clubs' medical staff will now ensure that not only are their players properly looked after, the coaching staff is too.A manager's life can still be a lonely place, but thankfully the help available is on a different level to where it was at the start of my career.Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

schema.headline: Tony Pulis column: Why managers must put their own fitness first
